title: Which habits matter at every stage of a case interview?
description: You are being judged on how you come across in every minute, not just the answers. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Four habits matter at every stage of a case: link every finding back to the client's goal, think out loud, keep facts, hypotheses and actions clearly apart, and stay calm when something goes wrong. Interviewers judge how you come across in every minute, not just whether your answers are right. These habits are what make you sound like a consultant rather than a candidate.
body:
Stage 10 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why habits matter as much as answers

Two candidates can reach the same answer and get very different feedback. One explained each step, tied it to the goal and recovered calmly from a slip. The other went quiet, drifted and looked rattled. The firms say as much in their own guidance. BCG's case interview tips include "show your thinking" and warn against panicking under pressure or staying silent. Bain's case interview page asks candidates to think aloud and to pause to gather their thoughts when needed.

1. Link everything back to the goal

Every answer, insight and calculation should connect to the goal at the top of your page. Make it a reflex to finish with:

"...and this matters because our client's goal is X."

For example: "Commissions are up $6M, which matters because that alone is more than the $5.5M we need to find to get back to $10M." If you cannot link a finding to the goal, ask yourself whether it matters at all.

2. Think out loud

The interviewer can only credit reasoning they can hear. Narrate your approach before calculations, your reading of charts and your reasons for each next step. Ask for time before taking it ("May I take a moment?"), then take it in silence. Thinking time you have asked for reads as composure; unexplained silence reads as being stuck.

3. Keep facts, hypotheses and actions apart

During a case you might know that a store's footfall fell 15%, suspect a new competitor caused it, and lean towards recommending a loyalty offer. Those are three different kinds of statement:

  • Fact: "Footfall fell 15%." (The interviewer told you.)
  • Hypothesis: "I suspect the new competitor is the cause." (You need to test it.)
  • Proposed action: "If so, a loyalty offer could win customers back." (Depends on the hypothesis.)

Labelling them clearly stops you treating an attractive early explanation as proven. It also makes it easy to change course when new data arrives. Changing your mind after seeing contrary evidence shows judgement, not weakness: "That rules out the competitor. The drop started before they opened, so I'd now look at our own changes." More on this in hypothesis-driven thinking.

4. Stay calm when things go wrong

Everyone makes a slip or loses the thread at some point. What matters is the recovery:

  • A maths slip: "Sorry, let me correct that: it's $3M, not $30M." Then carry on.
  • Lost the thread: "Let me take a step back. We know A and B, and we're trying to get to X, so the next thing to check is C."
  • A hint from the interviewer: take it gracefully. "That's a good point. If that's the case, then..."

Treat the case as a conversation between colleagues working on a problem, not an exam. Pauses are fine. A steady pace, a friendly tone and the occasional smile, especially when you are struggling, all help. For more, see how to come across as clear and calm and how to stay calm when nerves hit.

Business-sense habits that stand out

  • When you hear an upfront cost, ask about the running cost. A plant that costs $150M to build and $10M a year to run costs $250M over ten years, not $150M.
  • Separate one-off from recurring. A $2M one-off cost and a $2M yearly saving are not a wash.
  • Think about how people will react. Competitors respond to price cuts. Staff resist closures. Customers switch when prices rise.
  • Bring in a real example, sparingly. One relevant comparison from the real world makes an answer memorable.

Common mistakes

  • Losing the link to the goal. Glance at the goal box before every answer.
  • Going silent without asking. Ask for time, then take it.
  • Treating a hypothesis as fact. Say "I suspect" until the data confirms it.
  • Letting a slip snowball. Correct it in one sentence and move on.
  • Defending a wrong idea. When the data disagrees, change your view out loud.

Practise the moment

Say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. You have just given an answer about falling sales in one region. Add the habit that separates strong candidates.

Show a strong answer

"...and this matters because our client's goal is to get back to $10M profit within two years."

Why it works: Linking back to the goal shows you know why the analysis matters.

2. The interviewer mentions that a new plant will cost $150M to build. What do you ask?

Show a strong answer

"And what would it cost to run each year?"

Why it works: Investment cases turn on both the upfront and the ongoing cost. See payback and NPV.

3. You said the profit gap was $30M. The interviewer raises an eyebrow, and you realise it is $3M. What do you say?

Show a strong answer

"Sorry, I slipped a zero: it's $3M, not $30M. That makes it a much smaller gap, so the price rise alone might close it."

Why it works: One sentence to fix it, then straight back to what it means.

Where to practise next

The exercises on the interview skills page build these habits in a few minutes a day. Drill all ten stages with the flashcards on the perfect casing page, then put them together in a full case from the casebook.
